title: How Lehman Brothers Hid $50 Billion and Triggered the 2008 Financial Crisis
description: Lehman Brothers hid $50 billion of debt with Repo 105 — and filed the largest bankruptcy in American history on 15 September 2008.
script: At one forty-five in the morning, on the fifteenth of September, two thousand eight, a bank with [HL]six hundred and thirty-nine billion[/HL] dollars walked into a court in New York and told the world it was bankrupt. Lehman Brothers had survived the Civil War, the Great Depression, and two world wars. It had stood for one hundred and fifty-eight years. And in a single weekend, it was gone. The filing listed [HL]six hundred and thirteen billion[/HL] dollars of debts. It was the largest bankruptcy in American history, and it is still the largest today. But here is the fact that should frighten you more than the size. Three days before the filing, Lehman told the world it held [HL]forty-one billion[/HL] dollars of cash it could use at once. The truth, found later by a court-appointed examiner, was that only about [HL]two billion[/HL] dollars of it was actually free. The rest was already promised, pledged, or locked away. So how does a bank with six hundred and thirty-nine billion dollars run out of money in a weekend? And how did it hide [HL]fifty billion[/HL] dollars of debt, in plain sight, from its investors, its board, and its auditors? By the end of this video, you will see the exact mechanism. A trick with a dull name, Repo one hundred and five, that moved debt off the books at the end of every quarter. A bet on American houses, made with thirty-one dollars of borrowed money for every dollar of its own. And a final weekend when every buyer walked away, and the government said no. This is the story of the bank that was too connected to fail, and failed anyway. It started, improbably, in a cotton store. In eighteen fifty, three brothers from Germany, Henry, Emanuel, and Mayer Lehman, opened a small dry goods store in Montgomery, Alabama. They traded cotton, then moved into banking, then moved to New York. Over the next century and a half, the firm financed railroads, survived panics, and grew into one of the great names of Wall Street. In nineteen eighty-four, American Express bought Lehman. Ten years later, in nineteen ninety-four, American Express spun it off again as a public company, and a trader named Richard Fuld became its chief executive. Fuld had joined the firm in nineteen sixty-nine, at the bottom, and climbed for twenty-five years. On Wall Street they called him the Gorilla, because he fought for every inch and never gave ground. Under Fuld, Lehman changed. It stopped being a careful old bank and became a machine for turning American houses into Wall Street bonds. Here is how the machine worked, because this is the heart of the story. A family buys a house with a mortgage. Lehman, or a lender it owned, makes that mortgage. Then Lehman bundles thousands of mortgages together, slices the bundle into bonds, and sells those bonds to investors all over the world. Every step earns a fee. And the risk, the chance the homeowner stops paying, is passed along to someone else. It was a beautiful business, as long as house prices kept rising. So Lehman pushed deeper. It bought five subprime mortgage lenders, including two called BNC Mortgage and Aurora Loan Services, firms that specialised in loans to borrowers with weak credit. Lehman became the biggest underwriter of subprime mortgage bonds in America, the factory that turned the riskiest home loans into products the whole world bought. But origination was only half the bet. Lehman also kept enormous piles of the stuff for itself. It bought office towers, shopping centres, and apartment blocks. With a partner called Tishman Speyer, it paid [HL]twenty-two point two billion[/HL] dollars for Archstone, a company that owned more than eighty-seven thousand apartments across America. The day before the bankruptcy, Lehman still listed twenty-three billion dollars of real estate on its books. Now, to buy all of this, Lehman borrowed. And this is where you need to understand one word, because it is the word that killed the bank. Leverage. Leverage means borrowing to buy more than you could afford with your own money. Imagine you buy a house worth one hundred dollars with three dollars of your own money and ninety-seven dollars borrowed. If the house rises by five dollars, you have nearly tripled your money. But if the house falls by four dollars, your three dollars are gone, and you owe more than the house is worth. At the end of two thousand seven, Lehman held [HL]six hundred and ninety-one billion[/HL] dollars of assets, supported by only about [HL]twenty-two point five billion[/HL] dollars of its own capital. That is leverage of about [HL]thirty-one to one[/HL]. Thirty-one dollars borrowed for every dollar of its own. At that level, a fall of about [HL]three percent[/HL] in the value of what it owned would wipe out the entire firm. There was a second weakness, quieter than leverage, and just as deadly. The money Lehman borrowed was short-term money. It funded buildings and bonds that would take years to sell with loans that had to be renewed every morning, in a market called the repo market. As long as lenders trusted Lehman, the money rolled over, day after day, like a river. But trust is the only collateral in that market. The moment lenders doubted the bank, the river could stop overnight. And that is exactly what happened in September. JPMorgan, the bank that cleared Lehman's trades, demanded billions of dollars in extra collateral in a single week. Other lenders simply walked away. Lehman owned six hundred and ninety-one billion dollars of things, and could not sell them fast enough to pay the morning's bills. And the fall was coming. But before it arrived, Lehman built something to hide it. The trick was called Repo one hundred and five, and it is worth understanding, because it is one of the simplest frauds in financial history. A repo is a normal piece of Wall Street plumbing. A bank hands over some bonds, receives cash, and agrees to buy the bonds back a few days later. On the books, it is a loan. The bonds stay on the balance sheet, and the cash owed is recorded as debt. Repo one hundred and five changed one number. Instead of handing over one hundred dollars of bonds for one hundred dollars of cash, Lehman handed over one hundred and five dollars of bonds for one hundred dollars of cash. Under an accounting rule called FAS one hundred and forty, that extra five dollars flipped the deal from a loan into a sale. The bonds left the balance sheet. The debt never appeared. And a few days later, after the quarter had ended and the photograph had been taken, Lehman bought the bonds back and the debt quietly returned. It changed nothing about the real risk. It changed only the photograph taken on the last day of the quarter. And Lehman could not even get a legal opinion for this in America, so it ran the trades through its London arm, where lawyers would sign the paper. How much did they hide? At the end of two thousand seven, about [HL]thirty-nine billion[/HL] dollars. At the end of the first quarter of two thousand eight, about [HL]forty-nine billion[/HL] dollars. At the end of the second quarter, about [HL]fifty billion[/HL] dollars. The reported leverage looked like [HL]twelve point one[/HL]. The real number was thirteen point nine. And the auditors at Ernst and Young knew about the trick, and said nothing. So now you have the full picture. A bank borrowed thirty-one to one. It owned tens of billions of dollars of houses, apartments, and mortgage bonds. And at every quarter end, it used a paper trick to make itself look safer than it was. The only question was what would happen when house prices stopped rising. In two thousand seven, Lehman looked invincible. It reported a record profit of [HL]four point two billion[/HL] dollars, on revenues of nearly sixty billion dollars. Its shares traded above eighty-six dollars. The firm was worth nearly sixty billion dollars on the stock market. It was the fourth largest investment bank in America. Then the music stopped. House prices fell. Borrowers stopped paying. And the bonds Lehman had manufactured, and the buildings it had bought, began to lose value every single day. In March of two thousand eight, the warning arrived in the form of a corpse. Bear Stearns, another great Wall Street bank, collapsed in a weekend. JPMorgan bought it for [HL]two dollars a share,[/HL] and the Federal Reserve put up [HL]twenty-nine billion[/HL] dollars to make the deal happen. The government had just rescued a bank. Everyone on Wall Street assumed Lehman would be rescued too, if it ever came to that. That assumption would prove fatal. In May, a hedge fund manager named David Einhorn stood up in public and said he was betting against Lehman, because he believed the bank was lying about the value of its real estate. The shares slid. The lenders grew nervous. Then, on the ninth of June, Lehman announced a loss of [HL]two point eight billion[/HL] dollars for the second quarter. It was the first quarterly loss in the firm's history as a public company, and Fuld had to go to the market begging for six billion dollars of fresh capital. In the first half of two thousand eight alone, the shares lost [HL]seventy-three percent[/HL] of their value. August brought layoffs. Fifteen hundred people, six percent of the workforce, were told to go. Inside the bank, the third quarter was already a disaster. Losses on home mortgages reached [HL]five point three billion[/HL] dollars. Losses on commercial property reached [HL]one point seven billion[/HL] dollars. By September, the market had made up its mind. The only question left was whether anyone would buy the bank before it ran out of cash. The final week began on Tuesday, the ninth of September. Talks with the Korea Development Bank, the last outside investor still interested, collapsed over price. Lehman shares fell [HL]forty-five percent[/HL] in a single day, to seven dollars and seventy-nine cents. The next morning, the tenth of September, Lehman reported its third-quarter loss a week earlier than planned. [HL]Three point nine billion[/HL] dollars, the worst in its history. And Fuld announced a desperate plan. He would spin off between twenty-five and thirty billion dollars of commercial property into a new company called REI Global, and sell a majority stake in the investment business, including a respected asset manager called Neuberger Berman. The market did not believe a word of it. By Thursday, the shares traded at about four dollars. On Friday, the twelfth of September, the heads of Wall Street were summoned to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The Treasury Secretary, Henry Paulson, the Fed chairman, Ben Bernanke, and the New York Fed president, Timothy Geithner, told them the truth. There would be no public money this time. No rescue. If Lehman was to survive, the banks would have to save it themselves. Two buyers were in play. Bank of America looked, and then walked away, choosing instead to buy Merrill Lynch, another dying bank, for fifty billion dollars. That left Barclays, the British bank. Barclays was willing, but there was a catch. Under British rules, Barclays had to guarantee Lehman's trading debts until the deal closed, and that guarantee needed a vote of Barclays shareholders, a vote that would take weeks. On Sunday afternoon, the British regulator, the Financial Services Authority, refused to waive the rule. Barclays walked away. That night, Lehman's board met and voted for the only option left. At one forty-five on Monday morning, the fifteenth of September, the firm filed for Chapter Eleven bankruptcy. Six hundred and thirty-nine billion dollars of assets. Six hundred and thirteen billion dollars of debts. Twenty-five thousand employees. One hundred and fifty-eight years of history, ended by a weekend of noes. And then the panic began. On Monday, the Dow Jones fell [HL]five hundred and four points,[/HL] its worst day since the attacks of September the eleventh, two thousand one. The next day, the government that had refused to save Lehman agreed to lend [HL]eighty-five billion[/HL] dollars to AIG, the giant insurer, which was drowning in the same mortgage swamp. The same day, a money market fund called the Reserve Primary Fund, which held [HL]seven hundred and eighty-five million[/HL] dollars of Lehman paper, told its investors that a dollar in the fund was now worth ninety-seven cents. It was the first time in fourteen years a money fund had broken the buck, and about [HL]three hundred billion[/HL] dollars fled money funds in a single week. Within three weeks, Congress passed a [HL]seven hundred billion[/HL] dollar rescue package, the largest in American history. The recession that followed wiped out almost [HL]nine million[/HL] American jobs. While the panic spread, the pieces of Lehman were sold off like furniture from a dead man's house. Barclays bought the North American investment bank for [HL]one point seven five billion[/HL] dollars, and kept about nine thousand jobs. Nomura of Japan bought the Asian business for [HL]two hundred and twenty-five million[/HL] dollars, and the European business for two dollars. Neuberger Berman was offered to two private equity firms for about two point one five billion dollars. The reckoning came two years later. In March of two thousand ten, the court-appointed examiner, Anton Valukas, published a report of [HL]two thousand two hundred pages[/HL]. He called Lehman's accounts materially misleading. He found that the bank's executives and its auditors had hidden the truth about Repo one hundred and five. And he said there were grounds to sue Fuld, other executives, and Ernst and Young. In October of two thousand eight, Fuld had been dragged before Congress. A congressman told him the figure lawmakers had calculated, [HL]four hundred and eighty million[/HL] dollars in pay over eight years, and asked him a simple question. Was that fair? Fuld said the real number was closer to three hundred million dollars. What he did not say was that his [HL]ten point eight million[/HL] shares, once worth more than nine hundred million dollars, were now worth nothing. He was never charged with a crime. The creditors waited fourteen years. They filed claims of more than [HL]one point two trillion[/HL] dollars. By the time the estate finished paying, in September of two thousand twenty-two, it had returned [HL]one hundred and fifteen billion[/HL] dollars. In twenty ten, Congress passed the Dodd-Frank reform law, the biggest rewrite of financial rules since the Great Depression. So what is the lesson? Not that Lehman was uniquely evil. Plenty of banks made the same bets. The lesson is three rules about how banks actually die. First, leverage turns a small fall into a death sentence. At thirty-one to one, Lehman did not need a catastrophe. A fall of three percent was enough. If you borrow thirty-one dollars for every dollar you own, you are not investing. You are betting your life on prices never falling. Second, banks do not die slowly. They die in days, because they borrow short and lend long. Lehman's assets were houses and office towers that take years to sell. Its debts were overnight loans that had to be repaid every morning. When lenders lost faith, the money stopped in a weekend, and no pile of assets, however large, could be sold fast enough to replace it. Third, a bank's real asset is trust, and trust is spent in secret. Repo one hundred and five did not steal money. It stole belief. Every quarter, Lehman told the world it was safer than it was. When the truth came out, nobody believed anything Lehman said, including the claim that it had forty-one billion dollars of cash. That is why the bank died with six hundred and thirty-nine billion dollars on its books and only two billion dollars it could actually use. One hundred and fifty-eight years of history. A record profit one year. Bankruptcy the next. And the distance between the two was three percent, and one long weekend.
